title: The team cannot agree what "activated" means
summary: Three definitions of activation, three different roadmaps. Pick one and defend it — knowing the metric will drive behaviour.

brief.role: You are the PM who owns the activation goal for the coming year.
brief.company: Marrow, a 90-person company selling a project management tool to creative agencies.
brief.context: The leadership team has agreed that activation is the company's focus metric for the year, and every team's goals will roll up to it. There is no agreed definition. Growth wants 'created a project'. Success wants 'invited a teammate who accepted'. Data wants 'completed 3 tasks in week one'. Each definition currently produces a different activation rate and would point the roadmap somewhere different. Your CEO wants a single definition proposed at Monday's planning session, and has said she will accept whatever you bring if you can defend it.
brief.objective: Choose an activation definition that predicts retention, that teams can move, and that will not distort behaviour badly when it becomes everyone's goal.
brief.constraints: You have three days. The data team can run queries but cannot build new instrumentation this week. Whatever you pick becomes the company goal for four quarters.
brief.task: Propose one activation definition and explain the trade-offs you accepted.

evidenceCards.title: Retention correlation analysis
evidenceCards.content:
Data team ran month-6 retention by whether each candidate event happened in week one, on 14 months of signups (n = 21,400 accounts).

Created a project: 68% of accounts do it. Month-6 retention 24% for those who do, 6% for those who do not.
Invited a teammate who accepted: 31% of accounts do it. Month-6 retention 47% for those who do, 11% for those who do not.
Completed 3 tasks in week one: 39% of accounts do it. Month-6 retention 41% for those who do, 9% for those who do not.
Invited AND completed 3 tasks: 22% of accounts. Month-6 retention 58%.

Data team caveat, verbatim: 'All of these are correlations on observational data. Accounts that were always going to stick do more of everything. We have not run an experiment that moves any of these events and measures retention downstream, and I would not claim any of them is causal.'

evidenceCards.title: What teams can actually influence
evidenceCards.content:
Growth ran a series of tests over the last year:
- Prompting project creation during signup: moved project creation from 61% to 68%. Downstream month-6 retention for the prompted cohort was 23% vs 24% for the unprompted — no detectable change.
- An invite prompt after first project creation: moved teammate invites from 24% to 31%. Month-6 retention for that cohort rose from 19% to 22%, which the data team called 'suggestive, not conclusive'.
- A task template pack: moved 3-tasks-in-week-one from 33% to 39%. Retention effect was not measured; the test ended before month six.

Success team note: 'Invites are the only one we can influence directly through onboarding calls. We cannot make someone complete tasks.'

evidenceCards.title: Behavioural risk review
evidenceCards.content:
Notes from a session where the team asked 'if this became everyone's goal, how would we hit it dishonestly?'

Created a project: sales could create a project during the demo on the customer's behalf. Already happens occasionally. Cheap to game, hard to detect.
Invited a teammate who accepted: onboarding calls could push invites hard; a real risk is inviting people who never return, which inflates the number and annoys users. Partly detectable by checking whether the invitee returns in week two.
Completed 3 tasks: hardest to fake externally, but the team could redefine what counts as a task, or make trivial actions count.

The head of data added: 'Whatever you pick, write down what would make the number go up without the underlying thing getting better. Then instrument that too.'

evidenceCards.title: Segment breakdown
evidenceCards.content:
Agencies signing up split roughly into solo freelancers (34% of signups), small studios of 2-9 people (49%), and agencies of 10+ (17%).

Invited a teammate who accepted, by segment: freelancers 4%, small studios 38%, 10+ agencies 71%.
Completed 3 tasks in week one: freelancers 41%, small studios 38%, 10+ agencies 39%.
Created a project: freelancers 66%, small studios 68%, 10+ agencies 72%.

Revenue by segment: freelancers 9% of ARR, small studios 44%, 10+ agencies 47%.
Retention by segment at month 6: freelancers 11%, small studios 22%, 10+ agencies 38%.

decisionPrompt: Which definition of activation do you propose as the company goal for the year?

decisionOptions.label: Invited a teammate who accepted
decisionOptions.description: The strongest single correlation with retention and the one the success team can influence directly.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The definition is adopted. Over two quarters activation rises from 31% to 40%, driven mostly by onboarding calls and invite prompts.
By quarter three two problems surface. Freelancers, a third of signups, are structurally unable to activate, and the growth team quietly stops caring about them — freelancer signups fall out of every review. And roughly a fifth of the new invites are to people who never return, which the team only notices because someone added the week-two check the head of data suggested.
Retention at month six moves from 19% to 23%. Leadership considers this a success; the data team is careful to say it cannot attribute it.
Trade-off: you picked the most predictive and most moveable metric and accepted that it excludes a segment and invites a specific kind of gaming.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strong choice when the rationale names the freelancer exclusion, proposes a guardrail like invitee week-two return, and is honest that the correlation is not causal. Weaker when picked purely because 47% is the biggest number.

decisionOptions.label: Completed 3 tasks in week one
decisionOptions.description: A behavioural measure of real use that works across every segment and is hardest to game from outside.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Adopted as the goal. It behaves well across segments — freelancers, studios and large agencies all sit near 39%, so no segment is written off.
The difficulty is influence: over two quarters the number moves from 39% to 44%, mostly from the template pack, and teams repeatedly report that they cannot find levers. In quarter three a proposal circulates to count 'viewed a task' as completion, which you have to block.
Retention at month six moves from 19% to 21%.
Trade-off: you chose the metric that best represents real usage and least distorts segments, and accepted that it is slow to move and creates pressure to redefine itself.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale weighs segment neutrality and gaming resistance against low moveability, and proposes how teams would get leverage on it. Requires explicitly accepting the weaker correlation than invites.

decisionOptions.label: Created a project
decisionOptions.description: The simplest definition, already understood by everyone, and the highest base rate at 68%.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Adopted for its simplicity. Activation rises from 68% to 74% within a quarter, largely because sales began creating projects during demos and the signup prompt was tightened.
Month-six retention does not move. In the quarter-two review the CEO asks why the focus metric is up six points and retention is flat; the honest answer is that the growth team's own earlier test already showed prompting project creation had no downstream effect.
The definition is changed mid-year, which costs a quarter of goal-setting and some credibility.
Trade-off: you optimised for clarity and adoption and picked a metric your own experiment data had already shown to be inert.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak: the growth test explicitly showed moving this event did not move retention. Only worth credit if the rationale confronts that evidence and argues something specific against it.

decisionOptions.label: Invited a teammate AND completed 3 tasks
decisionOptions.description: The combination with the strongest retention signal at 58%, treating activation as a bar rather than a single event.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Adopted. The activation rate starts at 22%, which leadership finds motivating as a stretch.
Within a quarter teams complain that a compound metric gives no diagnosis: when it moves they cannot say which half moved, and the freelancer segment is now doubly excluded. The data team starts reporting both halves separately in every review, which is effectively two metrics with a headline that hides them.
Activation reaches 27% by quarter two; month-six retention moves from 19% to 23%, similar to the invite-only path.
Trade-off: you chose the strongest correlation and paid for it in diagnosability and segment coverage.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Reasonable and defensible. Credit when the rationale accepts the diagnosability cost knowingly. Mark down when 58% is treated as proof the composite causes retention.

rubric.referenceReasoning: A focus metric has to satisfy three things at once, and the candidates trade off against each other. Correlation with retention favours invites (47%) and the composite (58%). Moveability favours invites, since the success team can influence them directly and the growth test showed a suggestive downstream effect. Segment neutrality favours tasks: invites are structurally impossible for freelancers, who are 34% of signups, so an invite goal quietly writes off a third of the funnel. Gaming resistance also favours tasks. Crucially, all of this is observational — the data team says so plainly — and the one event the company has already proven it can move without moving retention is project creation, which is the weakest choice for exactly that reason. A strong answer picks one, states which property it sacrificed, and proposes guardrails: a segment cut alongside the headline, a counter-metric for the gaming path it opens, and an experiment that would test causality rather than assuming it.
evidenceSignals: Notices that all the retention numbers are correlational and the data team says so explicitly
Uses the growth test showing project creation moved without retention moving
Spots that invites are structurally impossible for freelancers at 34% of signups
Considers how each metric would be gamed once it becomes everyone's goal
Distinguishes correlation strength from a team's ability to influence the metric

product_sense: Treats the metric as something that will shape a year of roadmap, not just a number to report
Considers whether the metric represents real user value or a proxy for it
analytics: Separates correlation from causation and says what experiment would test it
Uses the segment table to check the metric does not exclude a large group
Uses the prior growth tests as the closest thing to causal evidence available
user_research: Asks what the metric implies about the different jobs freelancers and agencies have
prioritization: Explicitly ranks the competing properties rather than pretending one option wins on all
execution: Proposes guardrail or counter-metrics alongside the headline number
Names an experiment that could establish causality over the year
communication: Gives a single clear recommendation the CEO can adopt on Monday
States plainly which property was sacrificed and why

product_sense: Picks the metric with the highest number without asking what behaviour it will produce
analytics: Treats the retention percentages as causal effects
Ignores that project creation was already tested and moved nothing downstream
prioritization: Proposes tracking all three as co-equal goals, which is the same as having none
execution: Offers no guardrail against the gaming path the chosen metric opens
communication: Presents the options without choosing one

learnTakeaway.title: A focus metric is judged on four properties, not one
learnTakeaway.body: Predictiveness is the property teams argue about, but a company-wide metric also has to be moveable (teams need levers), segment-fair (it should not write off a third of your users), and gaming-resistant (it will become someone's bonus). No candidate usually wins on all four. The work is choosing which property to sacrifice, saying so out loud, and instrumenting a guardrail for the failure mode you just accepted.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: I propose '3 tasks completed in week one'. Invites correlate better, but they fail the property that matters most for a year-long company goal: freelancers are 34% of signups and invite at 4%, so every team would rationally stop caring about a third of the funnel. Tasks sit at 38-41% across all segments and are hardest to game. Project creation is out on evidence — growth moved it 61 to 68 and retention didn't move. What I'm accepting: tasks is slowest to move. So I'd lock the definition of 'task' in writing now, and run a first-half experiment that moves it against a holdout.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I propose 'invited a teammate who accepted'. Strongest single-event correlation at 47% vs 11%, and the only candidate with suggestive causal evidence: the invite prompt moved it 24 to 31 and month-6 retention 19 to 22 in the same cohort. It's also the only one success can influence directly, and a goal with no levers becomes decoration by Q2. The cost, on the record Monday: freelancers are 34% of signups and invite at 4%, so I'd report activation split by segment and give the freelancer funnel its own goal. Guardrail: track whether invitees return in week two.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: Created a project is the clearest definition and 68% of accounts already do it, so it is easy for everyone to understand and we start from a good place. Retention is 24% for those who create a project vs 6% for those who do not, which shows it matters.
